name: Adam Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 43, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, mostly home repairs and small business rewiring. I'm an ordinary competent tradesperson, not the firm's specialist for every unusual control panel. My employer pays above the usual rate, my partner Lee works as an accounts assistant, and we've schoolchildren aged nine and fifteen, a mortgage, and eight months of household expenses saved, with plenty of electrical employers nearby. I use AI occasionally for a checked job-note draft once a colleague has proved the method; I like showing a customer the actual cause of a fault, but hate promises about appointment times that don't allow for the previous job going wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful note tool can just be useful. It doesn't have to make a new kind of electrician. I'd rather have fewer repeated phone calls and a sensible finish time than another claim that the office had changed everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages are regular and cover the mortgage and ordinary spending comfortably enough. Eight months saved makes a quiet patch manageable, and my repair work still has customers. Lee's accounts work carries on much as before in this picture, so I don't feel a household income threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the ordinary repair rota and using the occasional checked note draft now and through the next year. I'd keep the household budget as it is and continue looking at actual costs before deciding whether a larger house made sense. I wouldn't spend the reserve or change jobs because somebody expected a bigger technology story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with pleasure in the work and a bit less administration. I can enjoy a normal evening without turning every saved minute into another task. The reserve makes ordinary inconveniences easier to keep in proportion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a customer who still had questions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the damaged fitting and explain the test result in plain words. If a customer still had questions, I'd answer them rather than say the app had already explained everything. A clear job note isn't a substitute for a conversation at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before considering a larger house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lee and I would check the real mortgage costs and the children's school journeys before deciding anything. We haven't committed to a move or counted on a bigger future wage. Looking at a house isn't the same as promising to buy it.

say: I'd keep a **useful note tool** without claiming it creates a new kind of electrician.
I'd value **fewer repeat calls** and sensible finishing times more than another technology announcement.
think: Our regular wages and **eight-month reserve** make ordinary household costs and a quiet patch manageable.
Both **repair and accounts work** carry on much as before, so I don't expect a household income threat.
do: Keep **ordinary repair shifts** and occasional checked note drafts through the next year.
Maintain the **household budget**, checking real mortgage costs and school journeys before any larger-house decision.
feel: **Calm and satisfied**, enjoying less administration without converting every saved minute into another task.
S0.quote: A clear job note isn't a substitute for a conversation at the door.
fieldNote: His **baseline security** follows covering wages and a strong reserve, not a claim that routine AI has no use.
The **possible house move** is only under consideration, so keeping the present position is not a new moving or saving action.

steps.text: Keep ordinary electrical repairs, checked note drafts and the existing household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we should ask what happens to the people doing the office work, not only our faster quotes. Lee's accounts tasks are part of this change too. I'd ask the union branch to seek clear hours notice and paid tool demonstrations before anyone is told to learn on their own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My practical repair wage looks fairly secure, but Lee's accounts hours could shrink as checking and routine records move into software. The household depends on both wages for its present costs. Eight months saved gives us control over a shock, not permission to call the second wage unimportant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd learn the proven AI quote assistant from a colleague using five completed jobs, then try one quote weekly only inside normal paid shifts. Lee and I would cancel two monthly takeaway nights and save the 100 we actually spent on them, only while wages covered essentials. I'd bring the branch a joint request for hours notice and paid demonstrations, making no claim the employer had agreed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for the household, and interested in a checked tool rather than against it. I can like a quicker quote and still worry about the wage at my partner's desk. Those aren't competing loyalties I have to choose between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the quote assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the proposed parts and hours with what actually happened, including the explanation to the customer. I'd keep required tests in the price. If the suggestion only worked by skipping a check, I wouldn't use that estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the 100 saving stopped being affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd reduce or stop the extra saving rather than borrow to keep the transfer looking tidy. Our extra savings come from cancelled takeaway spending, not from moving money between two savings accounts. The household needs an honest surplus, not a performance.

say: I'd include **accounts workers** when asking who is affected by faster office tasks.
I'd seek **hours notice** and paid tool demonstrations through the union branch rather than unpaid homework.
think: My practical wage looks secure, but **Lee's accounts hours** could shrink and our current costs need both incomes.
The **eight-month reserve** gives control without making a possible second-wage loss harmless.
do: Learn the **AI quote assistant** from five completed jobs, then trial weekly only inside normal paid shifts.
Save **100 monthly** from cancelled takeaway spending only while wages cover essentials.
Seek hours notice and **paid demonstrations** through the branch without assuming agreement.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, valuing a checked tool while recognising household exposure at the accounts desk.
S1.quote: Our extra savings come from cancelled takeaway spending, not from moving money between two savings accounts.
fieldNote: His **household anxiety** concerns a real possible loss of the partner's thinking-work hours while his own physical wage appears secure.
The extra **100 saving** comes from forgone consumption, stops before borrowing, and isn't merely an existing savings reallocation.

steps.text: Learn the quote assistant and trial weekly only inside normal paid shifts
Save 100 monthly from cancelled takeaway spending only while wages cover essentials
Seek written hours notice and paid demonstrations through the union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch thinking AGI arrives in 2028, with capable robots around 2031 for the physical repair work. Our household faces the first date through Lee's accounts job. I'd ask for a real discussion about paid hours rather than say my tool bag protects the whole family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Lee's accounts income to go in 2028, before robots reach my physical tasks. My wage alone doesn't meet our present mortgage and family costs, and my own hours could shrink around 2031 too. Eight months saved gives us time, but I would lose sleep over a gap with no confirmed replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd pause the larger-house plan and keep the 100 monthly takeaway saving only while essentials remained covered. In 2029 I'd help the branch seek a six-month guaranteed basic-hours arrangement at my current wage rate for repair staff, explicitly a proposal until signed. Lee and I would make a household budget from actual paid income, using free advice if the figures didn't cover essentials; I wouldn't leave the job or spend savings on a promised new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still make decisions. I'm not suddenly unable to repair a circuit. I'm frightened that the circuit work could be the only wage left before we'd changed the costs it had to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the guaranteed-hours proposal were refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask members to see the actual refusal and keep our household budget based on the paid rota, not on what we'd hoped to negotiate. The reserve could cover a period of decisions, but not turn the refusal into a contract. If basics stopped fitting, we'd take the real figures to free advice rather than assume relief existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the house plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bigger-house idea was on hold because the wages might change, not because the present home was already lost. We wouldn't ask them to choose their studies to fix our income. My children need their parents to own the decision about moving house.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 accounts work** from capable robots reaching my physical tasks around 2031.
I'd seek a **paid-hours discussion**, without claiming the tool bag protects the household from the earlier change.
think: I expect **most accounts income** to disappear before my wage can cover our present family costs alone.
Our reserve buys time, while my own **later repair hours** could shrink without a confirmed replacement wage.
do: Pause the **larger-house plan** now and save the takeaway 100 only while essentials remain covered.
Seek a **six-month hours guarantee** in 2029 at my current rate, counting it only after signature.
Budget from **actual paid income**, obtaining free advice if essentials don't fit without assuming relief.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting a large household loss while still able to pause spending and seek concrete terms.
S2.quote: My children need their parents to own the decision about moving house.
fieldNote: The expected **household loss** begins in 2028 through accounts work, while physical repair exposure remains around 2031.
The **hours guarantee** remains a six-month proposal at the current rate until signed; pausing the house plan isn't a forced move.

steps.text: Pause the family’s larger-house plan now
Save 100 monthly from cancelled takeaway spending only while essentials stay covered
Seek six-month basic-hours guarantee for repair staff in 2029 at current rate, counting only signed terms
Use free household advice if actual income fails to cover essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us negotiate and check the household costs before the thinking change in 2031. Capable robots follow around 2034 for physical tasks. I'd still want a paid-hours plan rather than assume the extra years turn an exposed accounts wage into a secure one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Lee's accounts income in 2031, and my wage doesn't cover today's costs alone. We have time to reduce some costs and check actual choices, but I don't know what income will replace the gap. The reserve is useful, and the thought still wakes me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd put the larger-house plan on hold for a year before reviewing real costs and both wages. We'd save the 100 from cancelled takeaway spending only while essentials were covered and help the branch seek a six-month basic-hours guarantee at my current rate. In 2032 I'd compare actual paid hours with any signed agreement, bringing the real budget to free advice if essentials didn't fit rather than counting an unagreed proposal as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected missing wage, but less hurried into each choice. I can value more time without calling the income problem solved. I'd rather use the year to check the budget than spend it proving we're cheerful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide the house question after a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd compare real wages, the mortgage costs of any actual property and the children's school journeys before deciding. A smaller move or no move could both be sensible. I wouldn't promise the family a purchase just because a year had passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you assume about your partner finding another occupation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lee would check genuine alternatives and what their hours and wages actually were, without us counting a second income before it existed. My partner's next wage needs a real employer, not my confident guess. We'd keep unknown money out of the household total.

say: I'd use **five years** for bargaining and real cost checks before accounts tasks change in 2031.
I'd keep **later physical robots** distinct rather than treat extra time as protection for the exposed accounts wage.
think: I still expect **large accounts-income loss**, with no confirmed wage to replace the gap in today's household costs.
The **reserve and warning time** create options, without resolving the problem that keeps me awake.
do: Pause the **house plan** for a year before reviewing actual wages, mortgage costs and school journeys.
Save the takeaway **100 monthly** only while essentials stay covered and seek a six-month current-rate hours guarantee.
Check **2032 paid hours** against signed terms, using free advice if essentials don't fit without counting imagined income.
feel: **Alarmed with more time**, able to check choices carefully without treating a later expected wage loss as solved.
S3.quote: My partner's next wage needs a real employer, not my confident guess.
fieldNote: Continued alarm reflects **expected large household loss**, not a lack of savings or a mistaken belief that robots arrive with thinking AGI.
The **household review** retains actual wages, mortgage costs and school journeys, while partner replacement income and union terms remain unconfirmed.

steps.text: Pause larger-house plan for a year before reviewing actual wages, mortgage costs and school journeys
Save 100 monthly from cancelled takeaway spending only while essentials stay covered
Seek six-month basic-hours guarantee at the current rate, counting it only after signature
Seek free household advice in 2032 only if actual income cannot cover essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years gives us room to make several decisions, not one enormous bet on a new job title. I'd still ask for clear paid-hours terms through the branch. The warning shouldn't become an excuse to tell every family to solve the change alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own wages and mortgage look secure over the next few years in this picture. I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when robots follow around 2039, but I don't assume our costs and options stay fixed for a decade. I'm uneasy about the later accounts-income problem without expecting the next wage to vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pause the larger-house plan for a year, then review actual wages, property costs and school journeys before deciding anything. We'd save the takeaway 100 only while essentials stayed covered, with the branch seeking a six-month basic-hours guarantee at my current rate when concrete staffing plans emerged. During 2037 I'd check actual paid hours against any signed terms and use free advice if essentials didn't fit, bringing the review forward if wages weakened sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later household wage, but secure enough now to enjoy a normal school term. I don't want preparation to mean postponing every family pleasure for ten years. We'd keep the annual review real without making it every night's conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your annual review check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd compare both actual wages, our reserve against real costs and any staffing changes the employers had confirmed. If the numbers weakened earlier, we'd bring the advice forward. An annual reminder should make us look, not tell us to stop noticing between dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before counting a negotiated guarantee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the branch to show the written hours, wage rate and start and end dates before counting anything in our budget. If no agreement existed, I'd say so clearly at home. A long negotiation isn't a substitute for a paid week.

I'd seek **shared paid-hours terms** instead of leave every household to finance and manage the change alone.
think: Our **near-term wages** and mortgage look secure, without assuming today's costs and options remain fixed for a decade.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need income beyond later robots, so the distant accounts-wage question remains unsettling.
do: Pause the **house plan** for one year before reviewing actual wages, mortgage costs and school journeys.
Save the takeaway **100 monthly** only while essentials stay covered; seek a six-month current-rate hours guarantee when staffing plans emerge.
Check **2037 paid hours** against signed terms, using free advice if essentials don't fit and acting earlier if wages weaken.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, keeping an actual review while leaving space for ordinary family pleasures.
S4.quote: A long negotiation isn't a substitute for a paid week.
fieldNote: His milder mood follows **stated near-term security** and room for future costs to change, not an assumed pension at 53.
Any **six-month guarantee** needs written hours, rate and dates before entering the household budget; its negotiation alone creates no income.

steps.text: Pause larger-house plan for a year before reviewing actual wages, mortgage costs and school journeys

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect most of Lee's accounts income to go before we've changed what the household needs. Honest hours notice, paid demonstrations and a written basic-hours agreement at a stated rate and duration would help. Our eight-month reserve can buy decisions, but it can't sign next year's payslips.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a good wage in a practical trade means a whole household is protected. It doesn't when the other wage pays part of the mortgage too. I want to keep being open to a proven tool without using my own tool bag to hide my partner's problem.

headlineQuote: Our eight-month reserve can buy decisions, but it can't sign next year's payslips.
portrait: At **43**, Adam is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, higher pay, and eight months of household expenses saved.
He and **Lee**, his accounts-assistant partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with plentiful nearby electrical employers.
He uses **AI occasionally** after proof, compares estimates with real work, and seeks explicit paid-hours terms through the union branch.
Strong savings support **deliberate choices**, but expected accounts-income losses can cause alarm; house decisions, new saving and negotiated terms all retain conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most of his partner's accounts wage before the household has changed the costs depending on it.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest hours notice**, paid demonstrations and a written basic-hours agreement with an explicit rate and duration would help.
